cues.text: In 1348, in Spain’s Valencia region, a priest from the parish of Alboraya-Almácera traveled by mule to bring Communion to sick parishioners.
This common pastoral duty was especially important during the years the Black Death swept through Europe, when he was suddenly swept from his mount crossing a swollen river.
The ciborium in his keeping was emptied in the fall, and the consecrated Hosts inside were carried off by the current toward the point where the river met the sea.
Barely saving himself from the water, the priest searched what he could of the riverbank but found nothing.
He returned home full of remorse over what had been lost.
Fishermen working near the river's mouth were stunned to see three fish break the surface and remain perfectly still.
Each held a small white disc, resembling a Communion Host, balanced in its mouth.
Word reached the priest, who returned to the spot carrying a chalice.
As the priest held the chalice above the water, tradition holds that each of the three fish in turn swam to it.
Each released the Host it carried into the cup and swam calmly away, before a crowd of witnesses gathered on the bank.
A small chapel, its door carved with the image of two fish, was built on the site of the miracle, and numerous documents testifying to the event have been preserved and can still be consulted today.

The fate of the three recovered Hosts themselves went unrecorded, but the story of the fish that would not let the Blessed Sacrament sink has been passed down in the Valencia region for nearly seven centuries.
